source.title: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models
source.authors: Tomer Porian; Mitchell Wortsman; J. Jitsev; Ludwig Schmidt; Y. Carmon

record.tranche_reason: The study reproduces and varies compute-optimal scaling experiments, showing that fitted allocation exponents change with FLOP accounting, warmup, and optimizer tuning; it also examines the shape and extrapolation of compute-optimal loss curves.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling sweeps, held-out losses, and loss-curve fits relevant to the claim. Related-work results cited from other papers are not recorded as findings from this study. Hyperparameter sweep values used to select settings are not cataloged as scaling-law outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study reruns IsoFLOP compute-optimal sweeps (16 models, 5M–901M, about 1.25e16–2.56e19 FLOPs, two datasets). It shows the fitted allocation exponent moves from about 0.83–0.86 to about 0.5 as head-FLOP counting, warmup and optimizer tuning are changed. It also fits saturating power laws to the compute-optimal loss and checks one larger-compute run. Neither original source is this paper, so verdicts apply.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors attribute the Kaplan–Hoffmann discrepancy to last-layer FLOP accounting, overly long warmup and scale-dependent optimizer tuning (batch size, LR, β2). With these fixed, they recover the Hoffmann (a ≈ 0.5) law even under a constant LR schedule, so careful LR decay is not needed. They add that tuned optimal loss fits a saturating power law, and that β2 tuning matters at small batch sizes.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an IsoFLOP-based compute-optimal analysis akin to Hoffmann et al., but does not replicate Kaplan's full setup: it uses OpenLM/Llama-derived models, different datasets and architecture details, and varies FLOP accounting, warmup, decay, and optimizer tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted compute-optimal allocation changes with whether the model head is counted in FLOPs, warmup duration, tailored cosine decay, and model-size-specific learning rate, batch size, and AdamW β2. The optimal-loss curve and its extrapolation also depend on optimizer tuning. Results are reported on RefinedWeb and OpenWebText2.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal batch size and learning rate follow power laws in N (BS ∝ N^0.703, LR ∝ N^-0.36). Tuning β2 is needed at small batch sizes for a clean trend (Fig. 3, Fig. 16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal optimizer hyperparameters scale as power laws in model size, and clean trends require β2 tuning at small batch.

record.problems: The authors note that their compute scale is much smaller than Hoffmann et al.'s and their model grid reaches only 901M parameters. Hyperparameter tuning targets smaller models and a 20-token-per-parameter training budget; OpenWebText2 runs may repeat data up to 4 times, and sweep data up to 10 times. Most optimal allocations and losses are estimated through interpolation rather than directly observed IsoFLOP minima. The extrapolation check is one model and one additional compute point.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant result rows omitted. Related-work results and hyperparameter sweep points used only to choose settings are excluded.

untested.parts: Loss as a separate power law in parameters or in tokens with the other quantity non-bottlenecked; only compute-optimal loss vs compute over about 3 orders of magnitude is tested.
Extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger; only about 3x beyond the fit range is checked.
Scales above 901M parameters and about 8e19 FLOPs; data other than RefinedWeb and OpenWebText2.
Entirely untested; aspect ratio is held at 32–64 and head count fixed at 4.
Entirely untested; the authors note downstream capabilities do not emerge at these scales.

missing.what: Allocation exponents with effective model size N_eff including attention FLOPs: a = 0.717, 0.622, 0.577, 0.505 across setups. The tuned setting predicts about 16B more parameters at Chinchilla scale.
Reproducing Kaplan's adjusted law with tuned hyperparameters plus head-FLOP omission and long warmup: a = 0.717 (Table 1) / 0.711 (Fig. 18), b = 0.289.
Estimated ideal per-ratio tuning shifts a from 0.483 to 0.457. Dropping the two smallest FLOP points gives 0.489 and 0.5.
Accuracy and confidence of the predicted exponent a as a function of total experiment budget (truncated FLOP grid).
Token-to-parameter ratio exponent r per setup, e.g. -0.668 for the Kaplan reproduction vs 0.006 tuned on RefinedWeb, and -0.74 vs -0.037 on OpenWebText2.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 label 'limits_scope' for R31 was reclassed: the single point agrees with the trend, and the orders-of-magnitude part is listed as untested rather than limiting. The R21–R30 loss fits also carry extrapolation claims, so they are linked to V2. The untuned saturating fits have irreducible terms (2.66–3.23 on RefinedWeb) near or above observed large-scale losses, consistent with the authors calling them poor.

versions.untested_parts: Does not independently test loss as a function of parameters or tokens with the other quantities varied to avoid bottlenecks; tests minimum held-out loss along compute-optimal allocations.
Tests one predicted point at about 8e19 FLOPs, not a run orders of magnitude larger than the runs used to fit the trend.

Tests compute-optimal model and token allocation on two datasets with models up to 901M parameters and compute budgets far below Chinchilla training scale; does not establish a universal trend beyond these settings.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Experiments are text pretraining; no other modalities, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling tests.
Tests sensitivity to model-size/FLOP accounting, warmup, learning-rate decay, and optimizer hyperparameter tuning; does not systematically vary all fitting methods, schedules, or data choices.
